Overview › How Pare works

How Pare works

Pare reads your TypeScript once, finds the parts that are only types, and writes the same text back with those parts replaced by spaces. It never builds a syntax tree and never prints code, so nothing it does not understand can be reformatted or lost.

  1. The lexer splits the text into tokens: names, numbers, strings, template literals, regular expressions, comments.
  2. The recognizer walks the tokens with TypeScript's own grammar rules (it follows parser.ts) and records which ranges are types. It writes down a list of ranges, not a tree.
  3. The eraser copies the source to the output, writing a space for every character in those ranges. Line breaks inside an erased range are kept, so line numbers never change.

If the recognizer meets syntax that cannot be erased, such as enum, the file is rejected with an error that names the line and what to write instead.

What "erase" means

You write Pare writes
let x: number = 1; let x = 1;
function f<T>(a: T): T {} function f (a ) {}
value as string value
interface A { x: number } (spaces, the line breaks stay)
import type { A } from "m"; (spaces)
import { type A, b } from "m"; import { b } from "m";

The full list is in Supported syntax.

A few things are not whitespace

In a handful of cases erasing alone would change what the program means, so Pare adds a character or edits an import:

  • import "./util.ts" becomes import "./util.js" in the CLI and in the MSBuild package.
  • A line that begins with ( or [ after an erased statement gets a ; so it does not glue onto the line above.

Output changes lists every case.

Why it is fast

The lexer and recognizer work on spans of the original text and write erase ranges into a buffer that is reused. While Pare parses it allocates nothing: no tokens, no strings, no tree. On checker.ts from the TypeScript repository (3.1 MB) it takes about 9 ms, around 335 MB/s. See Benchmarks.

Where the pieces live

Package What it is
Extrode.Pare the library: TypeStripper.Strip. No dependencies.
Extrode.Pare.Cli the pare command line tool, NativeAOT
Extrode.Pare.Build an MSBuild task and targets that strip .ts during dotnet build
Extrode.Pare.AspNetCore AddPareDevelopment(): re-strips on save under dotnet watch
libpare the same stripper as a C shared library, for other languages

Inside a .NET build

The output lives under obj/, never in your source tree, so there is nothing to put in .gitignore. The build keeps the .ts out of the published site and deletes the output of a .ts you delete.
